21639:
The critics share no single theology. Reformed scholars such as Meredith Kline and the Westminster faculty, two-kingdoms theologians, dispensationalists, Anabaptists, charismatic insiders and journalists all object to dominion programs, each for their own reasons.

Their common ground is that Christ's kingdom advances in this age mainly through word, Spirit and the church's witness, not by capturing civil power. On this view Israel's theocracy and its civil law belonged to a unique covenant that Christ fulfilled, the New Testament expects the church to live as pilgrims and often as sufferers until his return, and Christians serve their neighbours as citizens of pluralist societies while defending liberty of conscience for all. Most critics still affirm that Christians should take part in public life. Their dispute is about the standard, the means and the goal.

21654:
Criticism came in waves. In the late 1970s and 1980s Reformed scholars answered Bahnsen and Rushdoony, and dispensationalists answered both Reconstruction and Kingdom Now. In the 1990s sociologists such as Sara Diamond popularised 'dominionism' as a category for the Religious Right. Since 2016, and especially after 6 January 2021, journalists and scholars of Christian nationalism have focused on the charismatic Seven Mountains networks.

The critics differ among themselves. A dispensationalist and an amillennial two-kingdoms theologian agree that theonomy is wrong for opposite eschatological reasons. A secular journalist and an evangelical ethicist may both criticise Christian nationalism while disagreeing about almost everything else.

21785: Does Scripture teach that believers can claim health and material prosperity by faith and spoken confession, and where did this teaching come from?
21786:
The Word of Faith movement, also called the faith movement or positive confession, teaches that faith is a spiritual law. Believers who believe God's promises and speak them aloud receive what they confess, and God's will for his children includes physical healing and financial prosperity. Its line of teachers runs from the evangelist E. W. Kenyon in the early twentieth century, through Kenneth Hagin, often called the movement's father, to Kenneth Copeland, Frederick K. C. Price and many televangelists. A gentler 'prosperity-lite' version, focused on positive thinking and everyday blessing, reaches huge audiences through preachers such as Joel Osteen. Historian Kate Bowler calls this 'soft prosperity'.

The movement has drawn some of the sharpest criticism in modern evangelicalism. D. R. McConnell argued that Kenyon took key ideas from New Thought metaphysics. Hank Hanegraaff called parts of the teaching heresy. Gordon Fee and the Lausanne movement challenged its exegesis and its effect on the poor. Sympathetic historians and charismatic writers, among them Joe McIntyre, Dale Simmons and William DeArteaga, have disputed the genealogy and called for reform rather than wholesale rejection.

This entry sets out three positions: the movement's own teachers, its critics, and a mediating group of revisionist historians and internal reformers.
21788:
Word of Faith teachers hold that God has bound himself to his word, and that faith is the means by which his promises become reality in a believer's life. Faith believes in the heart and speaks with the mouth, as in Mark 11:23 and Romans 10:10. Words carry spiritual power, so believers should confess what God's word says, not what circumstances say.

The teachers hold that Christ's redemption delivered believers from the curse of the law, which includes sickness and poverty. Healing and prosperity are therefore part of the atonement, and believers stand in Christ's authority over the devil. They see God as a good Father who wants his children well and well-supplied so that they can be generous and spread the gospel. The movement includes a 'classic' faith teaching (Kenyon, Hagin), a more explicit prosperity teaching (Copeland, Price and many others), and a softer motivational form (Osteen) that keeps the optimism and drops most of the technical doctrine.
21790: Evangelist, Bible school founder, radio preacher, author
21791: Essek William Kenyon grew up in upstate New York. In the 1890s he spent time at the Emerson College of Oratory in Boston, a school critics link to the New Thought milieu. He founded Bethel Bible Institute in Spencer, Massachusetts (1900), and later ministered in Los Angeles and Seattle. His books on the believer's identity 'in Christ', the authority of the name of Jesus, healing and 'the two kinds of faith' became the main source on which later faith teachers drew, often closely.
21793: Pentecostal preacher, founder of Rhema Bible Training Center
21794: Hagin was a bedridden teenager in Texas with a serious heart condition. He said he was healed in 1934 after acting on Mark 11:23-24. He became an Assemblies of God pastor and then an itinerant teacher, and in 1974 founded Rhema Bible Training Center near Tulsa, which trained thousands of ministers. His plain-spoken books spread faith teaching worldwide. McConnell later showed that some passages closely reproduce Kenyon's wording. Late in life, in *The Midas Touch* (2000), Hagin criticised greed and manipulative giving appeals within the movement.
21797: Televangelist, founder of Kenneth Copeland Ministries
21798: Copeland worked as a pilot and driver for Oral Roberts and absorbed Hagin's teaching from tapes. He founded his ministry in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1967. *The Laws of Prosperity* (1974) and the *Believer's Voice of Victory* broadcasts made him the most prominent teacher of explicit prosperity doctrine. In 2007 his ministry was among six examined in a US Senate Finance Committee inquiry into the finances of religious nonprofits. The inquiry closed in 2011 with recommendations but no penalties.
21800: Pastor of Crenshaw Christian Center, Los Angeles
21801: Price was the most influential African American Word of Faith teacher. He was associated with Hagin from the early 1970s, built a large Los Angeles congregation, and taught healing, prosperity and positive confession on national television. He also challenged racism in the church in his later teaching.
21805: Osteen succeeded his father John Osteen, a Word of Faith-influenced pastor, in 1999. He built Lakewood into one of America's largest congregations. His bestselling *Your Best Life Now* (2004) presents an upbeat message of God's favour, positive declarations and personal improvement, with little of the movement's technical doctrine. Bowler calls this 'soft prosperity'. Osteen generally avoids specific doctrinal controversy and emphasises encouragement.
21806:
Faith teaching grew from several nineteenth-century streams. The Holiness and Higher Life movements emphasised the believer's victory. The faith-cure movement (Charles Cullis, A. J. Gordon, A. B. Simpson, Carrie Judd Montgomery) taught healing through the atonement. New Thought and Christian Science promoted the creative power of mind. Kenyon stood where these streams met. After the Second World War, the healing revivals and Oral Roberts's 'seed-faith' teaching on giving prepared a mass audience, and Hagin's Rhema graduates and Copeland's broadcasts spread the message from the 1970s.

It has since become one of the most widespread forms of Christianity in the Global South. A 2006 Pew Forum survey of Pentecostals in ten countries found large majorities in several African, Latin American and Asian countries agreeing that God grants material prosperity to believers who have enough faith. For many poor believers the message brings dignity, hope and a reason to work and save. Critics see the same reach as a source of exploitation.
21807: Faith is believing God's word in the heart and speaking it with the mouth. Believers receive what they believe and confess according to God's promises.
21808: Words have spiritual power, so believers should speak in agreement with Scripture rather than with symptoms or circumstances.
